top.headline: The Trump DOJ Quietly Intervened to Ink a Huge Payout to a Trump Golf Pro
top.blurb: Trump political appointees bypassed IRS legal review to approve a $500,000 settlement for a golf pro at Trump National Golf Club Hudson Valley — about 250 times the usual statutory payout for a tax-data breach — with two more plaintiffs tied to Trump businesses now seeking the same deal. Former officials call the process unusual, and the plaintiffs' lawyers say the class could eventually number in the hundreds of thousands, exposing the government to billions in liability.

top.headline: The U.S. Paid Insurers Billions to Cover Civilians Harmed in War. Even the Government Says the System Is Ripe for Fraud.
top.blurb: A ProPublica investigation found taxpayers paid nearly $5 billion over the past decade to insurers covering war-zone contractors, with annual reimbursements quadrupling since 2018 and a Labor Department memo calling the system "ripe for potential fraud." Four insurers collected the bulk of it, while the agency overseeing the program has no power to fine anyone or judge whether costs are excessive.

top.headline: U.S. Drug War in Mexico Fueled More Murders, Violence, and Drug Deaths
top.blurb: A new Tufts/Brown study shared exclusively with The Intercept finds the $3.3 billion Mérida Initiative coincided with Mexican homicides tripling and femicides rising 135%, warning that the Trump administration's expanding boat strikes and covert ops risk repeating the same cycle. Criminal groups now control roughly a third of Mexican territory, with U.S.-trafficked guns still their main weapons source.

top.headline: A US Religious Freedom Panel Says India Is Illegally Deporting Muslims It Strips From Voter Rolls
top.blurb: The US Commission on International Religious Freedom accused India of removing Muslims from electoral rolls, branding them "foreigners" and deporting them, with its chair citing Amit Shah's claim that three crore voters purged in the citizenship revision were "Bangladeshi infiltrators." The commission urged Washington to designate India a "country of particular concern"; India's foreign ministry has not yet responded.

top.headline: The Election Commission Can Blacklist a Rogue Booth Agent for Fake Voter-Deletion Forms. Nothing More, the Supreme Court Says.
top.blurb: The Supreme Court found the Election Commission essentially powerless against booth-level agents filing fraudulent forms to strike voters from the rolls, after a petition cited a Delhi constituency where one BJP-registered agent filed 37 such forms, 36 later found false. The bench ordered a probe but admitted blacklisting is the EC's only real tool, as similar bulk-deletion complaints surface in Uttar Pradesh, Telangana and Karnataka.

top.headline: India's Draft Rules Would Let Labs Pull Test Animals Off the Street. Scientists Say That Means Worse Science.
top.blurb: India's 2026 draft rules on animal testing would let labs draw subjects from shelters and streets instead of bred stock, relax anaesthesia and inspection requirements, and classify starvation as a "mild" procedure — reviving practices a 2000s-era crackdown had ended. Public comment on the final draft was also quietly restricted to NMC-registered medical colleges after the consultation closed.

top.headline: Hours After the Trump-Xi-Putin Summit, European Leaders Call It a 'Photo Op' and Push to Reopen Ukraine's NATO Bid
top.blurb: Meeting in Berlin hours after the Trump-Xi-Putin summit in China, European leaders dismissed it as a photo op, with Macron pushing to reopen Ukraine's NATO membership question and Kushner claiming Russia is "comfortable" with NATO-style security guarantees. Putin vowed retaliation for Ukraine's Kerch Bridge strike, and minor damage to Dutch and Austrian embassies in Kyiv underscored how fragile the diplomacy remains.

top.headline: Thousands Protest Colombia's Tax Plans Amid a Row Over the US Military Role
top.blurb: Tens of thousands marched against President de la Espriella's tax overhaul as reports surfaced that Bogotá rejected a US proposal for joint anti-cartel operations on Colombian soil, shortening Defense Secretary Hegseth's visit. The twin disputes — who pays for a fiscal crisis, and how far Colombia will cooperate with Washington — are fueling a second wave of nationwide unrest.

top.headline: El Salvador's Bukele Expected to Formalise Bid for a Third Presidential Term
top.blurb: Nayib Bukele is set to register for a third consecutive term after a 2025 constitutional amendment extended terms to six years, running on a security crackdown that has jailed over 1% of the population, often without charge. His approach is becoming a model for right-wing leaders elsewhere in Latin America even as rights groups document mass arrests and a jailed human-rights lawyer held incommunicado for over a year.

top.headline: South Africa Rout Bangladesh by Nine Wickets to Seize Top Spot in the World Test Championship
top.blurb: South Africa chased down a nominal target before lunch on day five in Johannesburg, Simon Harmer's 6/51 skittling Bangladesh for 168 after Kagiso Rabada's five-wicket haul in the first innings, to move top of the World Test Championship table. Towhid Hridoy's 137 and Litton Das's 120 had carried Bangladesh to a competitive 400, but captain Temba Bavuma, who played on through a calf strain to see out the win, now risks missing next week's second Test.

top.headline: Glenn Phillips Becomes First Batter to Score a Century Against India in All Three Formats in One Year
top.blurb: Glenn Phillips's 118 in the opening Test at the Basin Reserve made him the first player to hit a century against India in Tests, ODIs and T20Is in the same calendar year, following tons in Indore in January and Auckland in October. He and Henry Nicholls added 216 together after New Zealand had slumped to 70/5, with Nicholls going on to his 12th Test century before Phillips fell to Akash Deep.

more.headline: Pakistan Beat Sri Lanka to Claim Their First Test Series Win in Over Two Years
more.blurb: Pakistan chased down a small target after bowling out Sri Lanka for 316, sealing a 1-0 series win and their first series victory since beating England at home in 2024.

top.headline: 'Godzilla Minus Zero' Review: The Monster Battles Land, the Plot Mostly Doesn't
top.blurb: Takashi Yamazaki's sequel to Godzilla Minus One trades on its predecessor's reputation, with Scroll's review finding the kaiju battles thrillingly staged even as exposition-heavy plotting and heavy-handed sentimentality around a young survivor weigh down the human story. Visual effects look rougher than before, but the critic calls it enough of a "return on investment" to satisfy as a commercial sequel.

bengal.headline: A Zero FIR Accuses Two Former Bengal Ministers and 36 Others of Sexual Exploitation of Contractual Women Workers
bengal.blurb: Three contractual women workers in Bengal's Information and Cultural Affairs Department accuse former ministers Bratya Basu and Indranil Sen, and 36 others, of years of sexual coercion and extortion.

bengal.headline: A Kolkata Medical College Erupts as Interns Punished Over a Stampede Response Clash With Rival Student Groups
bengal.blurb: Interns show-caused over questioning a deadly stampede's hospital response clashed with rival groups at Kolkata's CMCH, as the health minister blamed "Naxalite elements" and doctors called the probe panel biased.

travel.headline: As Sri Lanka's Wild Animals Are Pushed Into Its Cities, a Rescue Center Logs Nearly 5,000 Cases a Year
travel.blurb: Habitat loss and vanishing predators are pushing peacocks, langurs and spotted deer into Colombo's suburbs, where one rescue center logged nearly 5,000 animal cases last year, most from roads or power lines.

happy.headline: At 93, Pablo Casals Explains Why Work — Done With Love — Is What Keeps You Alive
happy.blurb: At 93, cellist Pablo Casals — who once nearly died by suicide as a teenager — explained why he refused retirement: daily Bach, humility about talent, and work as "a salute to life."

tech_top.headline: ICE Is Paying AT&T to Dig Through a Mountain of Call Records
tech_top.blurb: An internal ICE document shows the agency is paying AT&T more than $2 million a year for a "Data Analytical Services" program that privacy advocates call Hemisphere surveillance by another name, letting investigators mine call records and location data via an administrative subpoena rather than a warrant. AT&T says the work is covered by valid legal demands; critics including Sen. Ron Wyden call it warrantless surveillance with no judicial oversight.
tech_top.pm_note: A case study in lock-in: once a sole-source vendor is the only one with a capability, a 'program' survives its own officially-announced shutdown — the same dynamic that makes migrating off an entrenched data vendor so hard inside a product org.

tech_top.headline: UK Government Forced to Disclose Secret Apple Backdoor Order
tech_top.blurb: The UK's Investigatory Powers Tribunal ruled the Home Office must confirm it secretly ordered Apple to build a way into customers' encrypted iCloud data, rejecting the government's national-security objection after rights group Liberty sued. Apple refused the order and instead disabled Advanced Data Protection for UK users rather than weaken its encryption everywhere, calling the ruling an overdue step toward transparency.
tech_top.pm_note: The sharpest live test yet of 'lawful access' versus end-to-end encryption: Apple's actual answer was to turn off a security feature for one country rather than weaken it globally — a tradeoff any PM shipping E2E encryption across multiple legal regimes should expect to face explicitly, not hypothetically.

tech_more.headline: Anthropic Hits Nasdaq at $111, 33% Above Its IPO Price
tech_more.blurb: Anthropic's shares opened near $111, a 33% pop over its $83 IPO price that briefly valued the AI lab above $2 trillion — behind only Apple, Amazon, Alphabet, Nvidia and Microsoft among US companies.

tech_more.headline: Google Gives Gemini the Ability to Use Your Mac for You
tech_more.blurb: Google added a "computer use" mode letting Gemini operate Mac apps and browse the web unsupervised for Plus, Pro and Ultra subscribers, following similar agentic desktop features already live at OpenAI, Anthropic and Meta.

tech_101.text: A records request a government agency can issue on its own, without asking a judge. ICE's AT&T data program runs on these instead of warrants — exactly what privacy advocates object to, since no court ever reviews whether the request is justified.

Governments sometimes demand a way to read encrypted data for investigations; companies that build genuine end-to-end encryption can't comply without weakening it for everyone. Apple's answer to the UK's order was to turn off the encryption feature for UK users rather than build the backdoor — a real-world resolution of a debate usually only discussed in the abstract.

science.headline: Why Hydrogen Flames Can Glow Orange, Then Turn Nearly Invisible
science.blurb: University of Adelaide engineers tracked hydrogen flames for two weeks and found their visible glow depends almost entirely on windborne sodium, from sources like sea salt, rather than the fuel itself — the sodium signal varied 28-fold between readings. Because hydrogen flames are far dimmer than natural-gas ones and can vanish to the eye entirely, the team argues appliance safety should shift from "look for the flame" to UV, infrared or temperature-based detectors.

science.headline: Mercury-Bound X-ray Telescope Delivers First Images After Eight Years in Space
science.blurb: ESA/JAXA's BepiColombo mission opened the eyes of its Mercury Imaging X-ray Spectrometer for the first time, training it on the Crab Nebula across 39 hours to calibrate it ahead of Mercury orbit insertion on November 21. The detector shows zero radiation damage after eight years in transit, and once operational will map Mercury's surface composition — the first imaging X-ray telescope ever flown on a planetary mission.

science.headline: More Than 1,700 Bee Species Are Unique to Islands, First Global Assessment Finds
science.blurb: A global checklist spanning 305 islands and over 600,000 records found 1,742 of 4,128 island-recorded bee species exist nowhere else, even though islands cover just 6% of Earth's land. The researchers say the same isolation dynamics likely apply to fragmented mainland habitats, making this a usable conservation framework beyond islands alone.

philosophy.headline: In Praise of the Dilettante
philosophy.blurb: Philosopher Jay Miller argues the dilettante — the deeply engaged amateur who refuses to specialize — is a defensible, even admirable way to live against a culture that prizes single-minded mastery. Drawing on Kierkegaard's aesthete and Nietzsche's free spirit, he reframes dilettantism as a mode of abundance rather than a lack of seriousness, while conceding it rarely brings recognition or acclaim.

philosophy.headline: Why Church-State Separation Rests on a Psychological Distinction, Not Just a Legal One
philosophy.blurb: Philosopher Neil Van Leeuwen and legal scholar Jacob Eisler argue that church-state separation rests on a hidden psychological distinction: "religious credence" doesn't update with evidence and stays compartmentalized to sacred contexts, unlike ordinary factual belief. That difference, not religion's subject matter, is what justifies keeping the state out of establishing belief while still protecting free exercise.

philosophy_101.text: A way of holding an idea that doesn't update with evidence and stays confined to sacred moments and rituals — unlike ordinary factual belief, which responds to evidence and governs everyday action. The distinction, not religion's subject matter, is what philosophers argue justifies keeping church and state separate.

Negative freedom is room to move within a practice without obstruction; positive freedom is the active drive to explore and make your mark. The dilettante, who roams across pursuits without being tied to mastering one, draws on both to justify a life of breadth over specialization.
